701.title: The House among the idols
701.hook: the Ka'ba of Ibrahim, now surrounded by idols, and pilgrims still came
701.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Hajj and the 'umrah call out the talbiyah, the pilgrim's cry declaring that God has no partner, as they travel to and circle the Ka'ba.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sha'ir, poets at the fair. Your line was: words had power.

Al-Lat. Al-'Uzza. Manat. Surah fifty-three names them, goddesses the Meccans honored. In the Mecca the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would be born into, figures like these stand around a stone house in a dry valley. And still, season after season, pilgrims come to walk around that house, circling it, calling out, leaving again for home. Who put the idols there? And who built the house before them, and for whom? The Qur'an has an answer, and it isn't any of the figures standing there. Today: the House among the idols.
screen: `AL-LAT. AL-'UZZA. MANAT.` → `A HOUSE, CROWDED.` → `AND STILL, PILGRIMS CAME.`

segments.voice: The house is the Ka'ba, a stone building roughly the shape of a cube. Surah two remembers how it began, in Pickthall's translation: "And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House." In surah twenty-two, Allah tells Ibrahim to purify the House for those who walk around it, stand, bow and prostrate. That was its first purpose. By the time of the Prophet's birth, the sirah says, it had filled up. The three goddesses had their own shrines elsewhere in the region, but at the House itself the sirah places a god called Hubal, whose name, Sahih al-Bukhari remembers, Abu Sufyan called out at the battle of Uhud. And Ibn Mas'ud reports, in al-Bukhari, that on the day the Prophet entered Mecca years later, idols stood all around the House, three hundred and sixty in his telling, and the Prophet struck them with a stick, reciting a verse that Pickthall renders: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away." That is the end of this story. Today is the cluttered middle. Even then, the House had not quite forgotten. Sahih Muslim preserves the cry the Meccans called out as they circled: here I am, O Lord, here I am, You have no partner. And then they added: except a partner who is Yours, whom You own, along with all he owns. The report says that when they reached no partner, the Prophet would say: stop there, enough. Pilgrims at the Hajj still call out a cry like it, the talbiyah, and in the version the Prophet taught, You have no partner stands with nothing added. Under the idols, the foundations were still Ibrahim's.
screen: `RAISING THE FOUNDATIONS.` · `AND A GOD CALLED HUBAL.` · `NO PARTNER, EXCEPT A PARTNER.` · `UNDER THE IDOLS, IBRAHIM'S STONES.` · then, large: `TRUTH HATH COME.`

segments.voice: Picture an old house with things piled on things, and walk through it until you find one wall that was there before the clutter; in your mind, put your hand flat against it. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you what has piled up around what matters in your own life; if you don't, simply notice what the clutter is covering.
Ka'ba. The stone house raised for one God, crowded with idols before the Prophet ﷺ, and still walked around by pilgrims today. Today's word.
Your line: the house remembered. Tomorrow, the hanifs. Day seven hundred one, done.

702.title: The hanifs
702.hook: a few people refused the idols and sought the religion of Ibrahim
702.howItsDone: The Qur'an calls its listeners to follow the religion of Ibrahim, the upright (3:95), and its verses calling Ibrahim hanif are recited in classes and sermons on pure worship of the one God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ka'ba, the House among the idols. Your line was: the house remembered.

A man stands with his back pressed against the wall of the Ka'ba, facing the crowd instead of the idols. Asma, the daughter of Abu Bakr, remembered him there, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps her memory. He is calling out to the people of Quraysh: none of you follows the religion of Ibrahim except me. His name is Zayd ibn Amr. No book of his own, no community behind him. Just a wall at his back and a refusal. Today's word is what people called someone like him.
screen: `A MAN, HIS BACK TO THE KA'BA.` → `NONE OF YOU BUT ME.` → `ZAYD IBN AMR.`

segments.voice: The word is hanif. Pickthall renders it upright; others explain it as one who turns from false worship toward the one God. The Qur'an uses it more than once for Ibrahim. In surah three, Pickthall translates: "So follow the religion of Abraham, the upright. He was not of the idolaters." In surah sixteen, Ibrahim is "by nature upright." Hanif is the word under both. So in a Mecca crowded with idols, tradition remembers a few people who looked at all of it and said no. No scripture, no congregation. Just a name, Ibrahim, and a conviction that the House belonged to one God. Zayd ibn Amr is one of them remembered by name in al-Bukhari, and the reports about him are concrete. He would not eat meat sacrificed to idols. His reason, as al-Bukhari gives it: God created the sheep, sent down the rain, and grew the grass, and still people slaughtered it in names other than His. Asma remembers, too, that when a father meant to kill his little daughter, Zayd would step in. Don't kill her, he would say. I'll feed her for you. Another report says he traveled north asking learned people about true religion, was pointed back to the religion of Ibrahim, and lifted his hands and declared that he was on it. The sirah says he died before the revelation began. So a hanif wasn't a member of a movement with a meeting place. Some readers describe the word as a direction rather than a club: someone already turned toward God, before there was a road to walk on.
screen: `HANIF: TURNED TOWARD THE ONE GOD.` · `THE RELIGION OF ABRAHAM, THE UPRIGHT.` · `NO MEAT FOR IDOLS. DON'T KILL HER.` · `A DIRECTION, NOT A CLUB.` · then, large: `BY NATURE UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Find one thing you hold to quietly, even when the room around you doesn't: that people deserve dignity, that a promise is a promise, that God is one, whatever is truly yours. Don't argue for it; just hold it, steady, not loud, the way Zayd leaned his back against that wall. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep you firm on it; if you don't, simply notice what it's like to stand on something.
Hanif. Upright: one who turns from false worship toward the one God. The Qur'an's word for Ibrahim. Today's word.
Your line: a few kept looking. Tomorrow, Zamzam found again. See you there.

703.title: Zamzam found again
703.hook: the sirah tells of Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather, digging out the lost well of Zamzam
703.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Mecca drink Zamzam water and walk between Safa and Marwa in memory of Hajar, and Zamzam water is carried home to share with family and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hanif: upright, turned toward the one God. Your line was: a few kept looking.

Dig. That is the whole message, at first, spoken by a voice in a dream to a man asleep near the Ka'ba. Dig what, he asks. The sirah says the voice came back on other nights, and finally gave him a name, Zamzam, and strange signs for the place: between the dung and the blood, where a crow pecks, near an ants' nest. The sleeper is Abd al-Muttalib, who would become the grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and he is being told to dig a well Mecca remembered by name, and nobody could find.
screen: `A DREAM: DIG.` → `A NAME: ZAMZAM.` → `SOMETHING NOBODY COULD FIND.`

segments.voice: Zamzam begins long before him. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas tells it. Ibrahim left Hajar and their baby Isma'il in the valley. The water ran out. Hajar ran between the hills of Safa and Marwa, looking for anyone, until she heard a sound and found an angel digging at the ground, and water came up. She began holding it in with her hands, building a little basin around it. The Prophet, telling this, said: may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; if she had left Zamzam alone, it would have been a flowing stream. In the same report, he says this is why people walk between Safa and Marwa. But wells can be lost. The sirah says that over time Zamzam was filled in and its place forgotten. Then came the dream. Abd al-Muttalib took a pickaxe and his son al-Harith, his only son at the time, the sirah says, and dug where the signs pointed, until the stones of the old well appeared. Then the hard part. The men of Quraysh came to him. This is the well of our father Isma'il, they said; we have a right to it. Give us a share. He refused. It was given to me, he said, not to you. The sirah says they set out together to put the quarrel before a judge, and that on the road, when the travelers' water ran out, water sprang up where Abd al-Muttalib's camel rose, and Quraysh gave way. From then on, giving water to pilgrims was his family's honor, a service the Qur'an itself mentions in surah nine.
screen: `HAJAR, ISMA'IL, AND THE WATER.` · `FILLED IN AND FORGOTTEN.` · `A DREAM, A PICKAXE, A SON.` · `OUR FATHER ISMA'IL'S WELL.` · then, large: `IT WOULD HAVE BEEN A FLOWING STREAM.`

segments.voice: Let one good thing come up that got filled in over the years, a habit you loved, a friendship, a prayer you used to say, the way the old stones came up under the pickaxe: is there still water there? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open it again; if you don't, simply remember it, and wonder whether it's worth digging out.

704.title: A hundred camels
704.hook: the sirah tells how Abd al-Muttalib's vow to sacrifice a son was ransomed with a hundred camels, and the son was Abdullah
704.howItsDone: The story of Abdullah's ransom is told in the sirah books and in mosque classes on the Prophet's family, and the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha remembers Ibrahim's ransomed son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zamzam, the old well dug out again. Your line was: the old well, found.

A vow, made in a hard moment. The sirah says that while Abd al-Muttalib was digging Zamzam, with one son beside him and the men of Quraysh against him, he promised God: if I am given ten sons who grow up to stand by me, I will sacrifice one of them at the House. Years pass. The sons come. They grow up. And a father now has to face a promise that has names and faces. Today: a hundred camels.
screen: `A VOW IN A HARD MOMENT.` → `TEN SONS, AND ONE TO GIVE.` → `A PROMISE WITH A FACE.`

segments.voice: He gathered his sons, the sirah says, told them of the vow, and they agreed. Lots were cast at the House with marked arrows, and the lot fell on Abdullah, the youngest, his father's favorite. He led the boy toward the place of sacrifice. And Mecca stopped him. Quraysh, and the boy's family on his mother's side, stood in his way: if you do this, they said, men will start bringing their sons here to sacrifice. Find another way. They sent him to a woman people consulted on hard questions. She asked what the blood-money was among them. Ten camels. Then cast lots, she said, between the boy and ten camels. If the lot falls on the boy, add ten more, and keep going until your Lord is satisfied. They cast. Abdullah. Twenty camels. Abdullah. Thirty. Abdullah. On and on, until at a hundred camels the lot fell on the camels. The sirah says he cast it three more times to be sure, and each time it fell on the camels. They were slaughtered and left for anyone to eat. Abdullah lived, and he would become the father of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Some who tell this story hear in it an echo of Ibrahim, who was told to sacrifice his son and was stopped. In surah thirty-seven, Pickthall translates that moment: "Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim." Ransomed: a life paid for with something else. The sirah leaves a picture close to it: a son walking away from the altar alive, and later, a ransomed father.
screen: `THE LOT FALLS ON ABDULLAH.` · `MECCA STANDS IN THE WAY.` · `TEN CAMELS AT A TIME.` · `RANSOMED, LIKE IBRAHIM'S SON.` · then, large: `WE RANSOMED HIM WITH A TREMENDOUS VICTIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a life that was spared, maybe your own in a near miss or an illness that turned, maybe someone you love who came through when they might not have, and let the memory come without the fear, just the fact of it: they are here, you are here. If you pray, you can thank Allah for that life in your own words; if you don't, simply let gratitude sit where the fear once was.

705.title: Abraha's elephant
705.hook: the Yemeni ruler's army marches on Mecca, and Abd al-Muttalib says the House has a Lord who will protect it (Surah 105)
705.tomorrow: a name no one had heard
705.howItsDone: Surah al-Fil, the Elephant, is short enough to be taught to children and recited in the daily prayers, and the story of Abraha is told in sirah classes as the prelude to the Prophet's birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abdullah, ransomed by a hundred camels. Your line was: a ransomed father.

An elephant kneels in the dust outside Mecca and will not get up. Its handlers beat it, the sirah says, then turn it toward Yemen, and it rises and walks. Turn it back toward Mecca, and down it goes again. Behind it waits an army, come to tear down the Ka'ba. In front of it, a town that has mostly fled to the hills. And somewhere between the two, a grandfather who has just asked a king for something nobody expected.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT THAT KNEELS.` → `AN ARMY AT MECCA.` → `A GRANDFATHER'S STRANGE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Abraha ruled Yemen, and the sirah says he wanted the pilgrims who went to Mecca to come instead to a great church he had built. So he marched north with an army and an elephant. On the way, his men seized the camels grazing around Mecca, among them Abd al-Muttalib's. So the grandfather went to see the king. Abraha, the sirah says, was struck by him, and asked what he wanted. My camels, he said. Abraha was taken aback. I have come to destroy the House that is your religion and your fathers' religion, and you speak to me of camels? And Abd al-Muttalib answered with the line this story turns on: I am the lord of the camels. The House has a Lord who will protect it. Then he went home, told the Meccans to take to the hills, and, the sirah says, held the door of the Ka'ba and prayed. The Qur'an tells what happened next in the surah called the Elephant. Pickthall translates: "Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant?" Did He not bring their plan to nothing, the surah goes on, and send against them "swarms of flying creatures", pelting them with stones of baked clay, and leave them like a field eaten bare? The Arabic there is ababil, and Pickthall renders it swarms. The surah never names what kind of creature they were. Years later, at Hudaybiyah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was riding his camel, al-Qaswa, toward Mecca, and she knelt and would not move. People said she had turned stubborn. No, he said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: she isn't stubborn. She was held back by the One who held back the elephant.
screen: `ABRAHA MARCHES ON MECCA.` · `GIVE ME BACK MY CAMELS.` · `ABABIL: SWARMS.` · `AL-QASWA KNEELS AT HUDAYBIYAH.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE HAS A LORD WHO WILL PROTECT IT.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've been guarding with all your strength, a plan, a child's future, a reputation, and for a few breaths do what Abd al-Muttalib did: look after your own camels, the part that really is yours, and loosen your grip on the rest. If you pray, you can hand the rest to Allah in your own words; if you don't, simply notice how much of it was never in your hands.
Abraha's elephant. The army that marched on Mecca, the elephant that knelt, and a grandfather's answer. Today's word.
Your line: the house has a lord. Tomorrow, a name no one had heard. Day seven hundred five.

706.title: A name no one had heard
706.hook: the baby is named Muhammad, the praised one, in the Year of the Elephant
706.howItsDone: Muhammad and Ahmad are given as names in honor of the Prophet ﷺ, and some Muslims fast on Mondays, following his practice and remembering his birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abraha's elephant, and an army turned back. Your line was: the house has a lord.

Someone once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about fasting on Mondays. His answer, in Sahih Muslim: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation first came to me. So the story begins on a Monday, in Mecca. The sirah places it in the Year of the Elephant, the year Abraha's army turned back. His father Abdullah, the ransomed son, has already died, the sirah says. His mother Amina holds the baby. And his grandfather, Abd al-Muttalib, gives him a name. Today: Muhammad.
screen: `A MONDAY.` → `THE YEAR OF THE ELEPHANT.` → `A GRANDFATHER GIVES A NAME.`

segments.voice: The name is Muhammad. Tradition says it was rare among the Arabs then. A story people tell says the grandfather was asked why he chose a name nobody in the family had, and answered that he hoped the boy would be praised in heaven and on earth. That story comes from later books, so hold it lightly. Tradition explains the name from the root h-m-d, praise, the root of al-hamdu lillah, praise belongs to Allah, the line the Fatiha opens with after the basmala. In that telling, Muhammad means the one praised, and praised again: the much-praised. The Qur'an uses his name plainly. In surah forty-eight, Pickthall translates: "Muhammad is the messenger of Allah." And it uses another form of the same root. In surah sixty-one, 'Isa, son of Maryam, gives good news of a messenger who will come after him, and Pickthall renders the name "the Praised One." The Arabic there is Ahmad. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet lists his own names, and Muhammad and Ahmad come first. Notice the shape of it. He is the praised one, but the root's first job, every time the Fatiha is recited, is praising Allah. The praise in his name points beyond him. And there's a small, warm instruction in al-Bukhari, too. Call yourselves by my name, he said. A name tradition calls rare back then is one you may well have heard today.
screen: `RARE THEN, TRADITION SAYS.` · `H-M-D: THE ROOT OF PRAISE.` · `MUHAMMAD AND AHMAD.` · `CALL YOURSELVES BY MY NAME.` · then, large: `MUHAMMAD IS THE MESSENGER OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Say your own name silently, and ask whether you know what it means, or who chose it and why; if you do, hold the meaning a while, and if you don't, hold the not-knowing, and the person who chose it for you. A name is often somebody's hope. If you pray, you can thank Allah for whoever named you; if you don't, let your name sound once more, gently, in your head.
Muhammad. The much-praised, from the root of praise, given by his grandfather, the sirah says, in the Year of the Elephant. Today's word.
Your line: the praised one. Tomorrow, Halimah's thin donkey. That's day seven hundred six.

707.title: Halimah's thin donkey
707.hook: the sirah tells how Halimah's donkey and flock grew strong once she took the baby home
707.howItsDone: Halimah is remembered by Muslims as the Prophet's ﷺ foster mother, and the sirah's account of her journey is often retold when speaking of barakah and of care for orphans.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muhammad, the much-praised. Your line was: the praised one.

A donkey so weak it keeps falling behind the others. A she-camel with no milk. A baby crying all night because his mother has nothing to give him. That is how Halimah, a woman of the Banu Sa'd, arrives in Mecca, the sirah says, in a year of drought. She and the other women of her tribe have come to find babies to nurse, because Meccan families sent their infants out to the desert, and the fathers paid. And there's one baby nobody wants. Today: barakah.
screen: `A YEAR OF DROUGHT.` → `A DONKEY THAT LAGS BEHIND.` → `ONE BABY NOBODY WANTS.`

segments.voice: The baby is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and his father is dead. In Ibn Ishaq's telling, Halimah says every woman was offered him and turned him down, because an orphan's family couldn't be expected to pay much. Every other woman finds a nursling. Halimah doesn't. She doesn't want to be the only one riding home with empty arms, so she tells her husband she will go back and take the orphan. He answers, the sirah says, that perhaps God will bless them through him. Then the story turns. As soon as she holds the boy, she has milk enough for him and for her own son, and both sleep. Her husband goes out to the old she-camel and finds her full. On the road home, the thin donkey that lagged on the way in now outpaces the whole caravan, and the other women call out: isn't this the same animal? Back in the dry hills of Banu Sa'd, her sheep come home full of milk while the neighbors' flocks come back hungry, until the neighbors tell their shepherds to graze wherever Halimah's shepherd grazes. The Arabic word for what fills this story is barakah: blessing, increase, good that stays. Notice where it begins. Not with a reward for a clever choice, but with a woman taking the child nobody else took, almost out of embarrassment. These stories come from the sirah, not the Qur'an, and later writers told them warmly. But the Qur'an itself remembers the orphan. In surah ninety-three, Pickthall translates: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?"
screen: `EVERY WOMAN TURNED HIM DOWN.` · `SHE TAKES THE ORPHAN.` · `MILK, A FULL CAMEL, A FAST DONKEY.` · `BARAKAH: GOOD THAT STAYS.` · then, large: `DID HE NOT FIND THEE AN ORPHAN AND PROTECT (THEE)?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose arrival made your life fuller in a way you didn't plan: a child, a neighbor, a friend who came in through a side door, someone you took on because no one else would. Let their face come clearly, and notice what grew after they came. If you pray, you can thank Allah for them by name; if you don't, just stay with the fullness and the face.
Barakah: blessing, increase, good that stays, the word the sirah uses for what filled Halimah's story when she took the baby nobody wanted. Today's word.
Your line: blessing came with him. Tomorrow, the opening of the chest. Day seven hundred seven.
